column2: Where wealth, youth, or learning dwells, there arises constant pride in age and also stupidity.
Ah, who can describe the greatness of gold! By mere likeness of name, the thorn-apple too (dhattura, "gold") gives intoxication.
If a wicked man gets wealth, that very wealth destroys the world, as wind is the friend of fire and poison the serpent's.
Ah, blinded by the pride of wealth, a man sees yet does not see; if he does see what is good for him, he truly sees, without doubt.
Having said this, the angry Kapila released fire from his eyes; that fire reduced all the sons of Sagara to ashes in a moment.
Seeing the fire from his eyes, the dwellers of the nether world took it for untimely destruction and cried out in grief and weariness.
Scorched by that fire, serpents and demons all quickly entered the ocean; the wrath of the good is hard to bear.
Then a divine messenger came to that king at the sacrifice and told him the whole event.
Hearing these words, Sagara, the all-knowing lord, was greatly delighted and said, "The wicked have been taught by fate."
Whether mother, father, brother or son, whoever does unrighteousness is considered an enemy.
One who delights in unrighteousness and opposes all the world should be known as the supreme enemy; this is the conclusion of the scriptures.
Sagara, the lord of sages, did not grieve even at the death of his sons, for the destruction of the evil-doers is a cause of the good men's cheer.
Since the sonless have no right to sacrifices, as tradition says, the lord took his grandson Amshuman as a son.
He then again sent the wise son of Asamanja, best of the eloquent and knowing the essence, on the errand of bringing back the horse.
He went to the door of that hole, and seeing that best of sages, Kapila, a mass of radiance, bowed with eight-limbed prostration.
With folded hands, humble, standing before him, he addressed the God of gods, the tranquil-minded, eternal one.
Amshuman said: "O Brahmin, forgive the evil conduct my uncles committed; good men, intent on helping others, have forbearance as their essence.
The good show compassion even toward wicked beings; the moon does not withdraw its light from the dwelling of an outcaste.
Even when harmed, a good man brings happiness to all; the moon, though devoured by the immortals, gives them highest satisfaction.
Sandalwood, though cut and torn, spreads fragrance everywhere; so too does the good man.
By forbearance, austerity and conduct, the lords of sages who know your qualities know you, O Supreme Person, as born to rule the worlds.
Homage to you, O sage, homage to you, embodiment of Brahman, devoted to Brahmins, intent on meditation on Brahman."
Thus praised, the sage, with a gracious face, said: "Choose a boon; I am pleased with you, O sinless one."
When the sage had thus spoken, Amshuman bowed and said: "Lead my ancestors to Brahma's world."
Then the sage, greatly pleased with him, said respectfully: "Your grandson will bring the Ganga and lead your ancestors to heaven.
The Ganga, the river of holy water brought down by your grandson, will cleanse them of sin and take them to the highest state.
Take this horse, child, so that the sacrifice may be complete." He reached his grandfather and reported the matter with the horse.
Sagara, with that animal, performed the sacrifice with the Brahmins, and by austerity worshipped Vishnu and went to Hari's abode.
To Amshuman was born a son named Dilipa; from him was born Bhagiratha, who brought down the Ganga from heaven.
Pleased with Bhagiratha's austerity, Brahma gave him the Ganga, O sage; Bhagiratha wondered how she could be borne.
Then, having propitiated Shiva, he brought the golden river to earth by him, and by touching her waters purified his ancestors and led them to heaven.
In Bhagiratha's lineage was born a king named Sudasa, whose son was Mitrasaha, famed in all the worlds.
Through Vasishtha's curse the king Saudasa took a demon's body, and was freed again by the touch of a drop of Ganga water.
He performs the rites told in the mantras... The god Shiva, teacher of the whole world, was worshipped by me.
By the disrespect I showed my teacher I was set in a demon's state; whoever shows disrespect to his teacher, knowingly or unknowingly,
quickly loses intellect, learning, wealth, children and rites. But the man who serves his teachers with respect —
prosperity comes to him, O king, say the wise. Burned by that curse, and by the fire of hunger within,
I do not know when I shall reach liberation, O best of kings." While this was being said by the demon seated in the banyan tree,
through their talk on dharma-scripture the sin of those two was destroyed. Just then a very righteous Brahmin arrived,
born in the Kalinga country, named Garga, carrying Ganga water on his shoulder, praising the Lord of the universe,
singing his names, his body bristling with joy. Seeing the sage come, the female ghoul and the demon,
saying "Here is our meal," ran toward him with raised arms; but hearing the names he sang, they stood far off, unable to attack him, and the demons said:

O Brahmin of great fortune, homage to you, great soul! By the greatness of chanting the names, we demons keep at a distance.
naradapuran:8:117	We devoured ten million thousand Brahmins before; the armour of the Name protects you from great fear.
naradapuran:8:118	By merely hearing the Name, even we demons have reached supreme peace, through the greatness of Achyuta.
naradapuran:8:119	In every way, O fortunate one, you are free of passion and the rest. By sprinkling Ganga water, save us from this heap of sins.
naradapuran:8:120	One who, becoming another to Hari (a servant), saves himself will save the whole world, say the wise.
naradapuran:8:121	Abandoning Hari's name, the medicine for terrible samsara, by what means can liberation, hard to get anywhere, be gained?
naradapuran:8:122	As one crossing on a boat of iron sinks in the water, how can those who have no merit save others?
naradapuran:8:123	Ah, the conduct of the great brings happiness to all the world, as the moon rises for the joy of all.
naradapuran:8:124	All the holy places on earth, O best of Brahmins, are equal to a single drop of the Ganga.
naradapuran:8:125	Ganga water mixed with even a mustard-seed's worth of tulsi leaf purifies twenty-one generations of a family.
naradapuran:8:126	Therefore, O Brahmin of great fortune, knower of the meaning of all scriptures, save us sinners by giving us Ganga water.
Hearing the supreme greatness of the Ganga told by those demons, the best of Brahmins was filled with wonder.
Even these have such devotion to the Ganga, mother of the world; what then of the great and meritorious who have the power of knowledge?
Then that best of Brahmins resolved in mind that the devotee who does good to all attains the highest state.
Then the Brahmin, moved by compassion, sprinkled on them the excellent Ganga water mixed with tulsi leaf.
Sprinkled by a drop no bigger than a mustard seed, the demons shed their demon nature and became like gods.
They went to the Brahmin, bowing well; they became chiefs of the gods, bright as ten million suns,
bearing the marks of conch, discus and mace, attaining likeness to Hari. Praising the Brahmin, they went to Hari's abode.
King Kalmashapada, restored to his own form, fell into deep thought on seeing those sinners go to liberation.
To that king in great sorrow, Sarasvati, unseen, spoke in a deep voice the great saying rooted in dharma:

O king of great fortune, you need not grieve; at the end of your portion, great good will come to you.
naradapuran:8:137	Those who have shaken off sin by good deeds and are devoted to Hari's worship go, without doubt, to Vishnu's supreme abode.
naradapuran:8:138	Those who show compassion to all beings, follow the path of dharma and honour their teachers go to the highest place.
Hearing this from Sarasvati, the best of kings found peace of mind and remembered his teacher's words.
Praising his teacher and Hari, greatly delighted, he told the Brahmin the whole earlier story.
Then the king bowed to the Kalingan sage, and, uttering Vishnu's names, went at once to Varanasi.
Having bathed there in the Ganga for six months and seen Shiva, he was freed from the Brahmin woman's curse and became Mitrasaha again.
Then he reached his own city, was consecrated by the great Vasishtha, O best of sages, and ruled his own kingdom.
Having ruled the whole earth and enjoyed pleasures, though without a wife, and having received offspring from Vasishtha, the best of kings attained liberation.
It is no wonder, O best of Brahmins: a man who speaks, hears and remembers the virtues of Varanasi and Vishnu, and drinks the Ganga, becomes free.
Therefore the greatness of the Ganga cannot be fathomed, even by the lords of gods, Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
By merely remembering whose name a man, freed from millions of great sins, goes to Brahma's abode, without doubt.
When the name "Ganga, Ganga" is uttered even once, at that moment he is freed from sin and honoured in Brahma's world.
